questions.title: What You Own Today
questions.question: Which of these sounds most like your portfolio right now?
questions.helperText: Choose up to two. It does not have to be perfectly organized yet.

options.label: Most of my money is in broad ETFs or index funds, and I mostly leave them alone.
I mainly invest through a 401(k), IRA, target-date fund, or another simple retirement setup.
I own ETFs plus a few individual stocks, but I am not sure whether they fit together.
I have started adding sectors, themes, dividend funds, real estate, or other investments.
I have several investments, but I would not say I have one clear strategy behind them.
I regularly compare allocations, rebalance, or look for ways to improve the portfolio.
I keep some money for stocks or opportunities that I think could outperform.
I have money ready to invest, but I am still trying to figure out where to start.

questions.title: Why You Are Here
questions.question: What question keeps coming back when you look at your investments?
questions.helperText: Choose the one or two thoughts that sound most familiar.

options.label: Am I actually doing this right?
Is what I already own good enough for the long term?
Are broad ETFs enough, or am I missing something important?
Am I overcomplicating something that could be simple?
When does ‘just keep investing’ stop being enough?
Why do some portfolios perform better than others?
When should I actually change something—and when should I leave it alone?
How can I pursue more growth without feeling like I am gambling?

questions.title: What Feels Sensible to You
questions.question: Which statements sound most like your view of investing?
questions.helperText: Choose up to two ideas you could realistically follow through both good and bad markets.

options.label: Investing consistently matters more than finding the perfect time or perfect investment.
A simple, diversified portfolio is probably enough for most of my money.
I am comfortable with average market returns if the system is simple and dependable.
A few well-chosen strategies can improve returns if they are applied consistently.
I do not want my future to depend too heavily on one company, sector, or country.
It makes sense to keep a stable core and use a smaller amount for higher-growth ideas.
Protecting what I have built matters as much as growing it.
Large market drops can create opportunities worth acting on.

questions.title: How Much Work You Want
questions.question: How much time and attention do you realistically want investing to require?
questions.helperText: Choose the one approach you would maintain for years—not what sounds most advanced.

options.label: Set it up, automate it, and check it about once a year.
Check in a few times a year and make small changes only when needed.
Review the allocation periodically and rebalance using clear rules.
Research before making changes, but I do not want investing to become a second job.
Compare funds, strategies, and portfolio approaches to look for improvements.
Follow new ideas and use a limited part of the portfolio to explore them.
Follow markets closely and make decisions when opportunities appear.
I want the system to tell me when something actually needs my attention.

questions.title: What You Would Do in a Market Drop
questions.question: If your portfolio fell sharply, which reaction would be most like you?
questions.helperText: Choose the reaction you would probably have, not what an ideal investor is supposed to do.

options.label: Keep investing and avoid changing anything just because prices fell.
Check whether my original plan still makes sense before touching anything.
Rebalance if part of the portfolio moved outside its intended range.
Move some money toward safer or more dependable investments.
Look for investments that may now be available at better prices.
Read what other investors are doing before I decide.
Start wondering whether I chose the wrong portfolio in the first place.
Move quickly if I believe the market environment has genuinely changed.

questions.title: When You Need the Money
questions.question: When might you need to use a meaningful portion of this money?
questions.helperText: Think about the money you want AaronBux to help you organize.

options.label: Probably not for at least 15 years.
Roughly 10–15 years from now.
Roughly 5–10 years from now.
Within about 3–5 years.
Within the next 3 years.
I have different goals with different timelines.
I am not sure yet. I mainly want to stop leaving the money unplanned.

questions.title: What You Need the Portfolio to Do
questions.question: What do you most want this portfolio to help you accomplish?
questions.helperText: Choose up to two. Your goals shape the portfolio, but they do not erase the behavior shown in your earlier answers.

options.label: Build wealth steadily without needing to think about the market all the time.
Know that my portfolio is properly diversified and not dependent on one big bet.
Improve my returns using a clear, repeatable strategy.
Keep a stable foundation while leaving room for higher-growth ideas.
Generate dependable income from part of the portfolio.
Protect money I have already built or will need in the future.
Turn the investments I already own into one organized system.
Act on market opportunities while keeping the risks controlled.
Feel confident enough to stop second-guessing every decision.
One balanced portfolio with growth, stability, cash, and room for selected opportunities.
A broad, low-cost portfolio that owns markets across countries and largely stays untouched.

ft_vs_ga.question: Which kind of improvement interests you more?

options.label: Using repeatable strategies such as value, quality, or momentum.
Adding new return sources such as private assets, real assets, or innovation exposure.

ga_vs_to.question: How do you want opportunities to enter the portfolio?

options.label: Through a limited sleeve that stays within a long-term allocation.
Through active decisions based on price, market conditions, or catalysts.

preservation.question: What are you primarily trying to protect or produce?

options.label: My ability to generate dependable income.
My purchasing power if inflation remains high.
Money earmarked for a known future expense.
Wealth concentrated in property, a business, or another major asset.
My portfolio across several different economic environments.

growth_specialization.question: What kind of opportunity do you want beyond a traditional portfolio?

options.label: Innovation and technology.
Private markets and multiple alternative return sources.
Property, infrastructure, and tangible assets.
Commodities and resource cycles.
Diversification away from a business or concentrated wealth source.

goal_bucket.question: Which timeline should shape the first portfolio blueprint?

options.label: A goal within the next 3 years.
A goal roughly 3–10 years away.
Long-term wealth more than 10 years away.
I need separate near-, medium-, and long-term buckets.
